segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Ima Hodge Platz came to the Palouse area with her parents from Missouri in 1900 and cooked for a number of years in the harvest fields. Here she describes cutting, shocking, and thrashing grain and the art involved and also cooking for the harvest crew.

segments.speaker: Ima Hodge Platz
segments.words: It was done in the crew and everything. We had thirty-two men to cook for three meters a day.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: When you were talking about how from the beginning when the grain is first cut, do you describe that to me again?

segments.speaker: Ima Hodge Platz
segments.words: Well, when it's first cut, it's cut with the binder. You know what a binder is. I've seen the pictures of them.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Oh, you never did see one, huh?

segments.speaker: Ima Hodge Platz
segments.words: No. Well, they have to cut. Sometimes they head grain. And then when they do that, well, that's a different set up, too, when they head it.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: But with the binder, then how does that do it?

segments.speaker: Ima Hodge Platz
segments.words: Well, with the binder, why they go around the field and they cut the grain, cut it off. It's a sickle. It cuts it. And then your binder, your bundles are made so they'll be the same size, you see. And then the binder kicks those bundles out. Then you go around and go up. They're pulled up, elevated up. And they keep, that'll go around and as your sickle goes across your grain, then that takes it up and then when you can set it, your binder. So your bundles will be the certain size, you know, that you want. There only.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: About two feet wide, a foot wide?

segments.speaker: Ima Hodge Platz
segments.words: Well, there, the height of the grain is, high as your grain is. But those, the twine that ties the bundles, it goes through the center of the bundle. And that's cut off and you've got the heads on one end and your stubs on the other where it's cut from the grain.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: And it's tied with twine at the same time?

segments.speaker: Ima Hodge Platz
segments.words: Yes, it's tied with the twine. The binder cuts it off and it gets a certain amount, but then it's adjusted so that it'll kick that out. I don't know, I guess they track. There's, well, if it never gets so full, why it's made that they'll kick it out, you know. And then your bundles will roll around on the ground.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Okay, then what happens?

segments.speaker: Ima Hodge Platz
segments.words: Well, and then ever who, you have to get someone to shock that up. And they get, there's about seven or eight of those bundles put in the shock.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Would you know how to shock one?

segments.speaker: Ima Hodge Platz
segments.words: I would know how to do it. Those bundles, you know, the bundles are the height of the grain that's cut. And that twine tied around the middle. And that binder kicks it out. And it'll cut more and it'll go in your binder. It'll come right through your binder and ties that grain up, you know, in a certain size bundle.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Then so many bundles make a shock?

segments.speaker: Ima Hodge Platz
segments.words: Yes, they can put so many. It all depends on how many bundles they put into the shock. It depends on the condition that the grain's in. If it needs to be aired out a little more or something, maybe they won't make such big shocks. Sometimes the grain is just shocked. Two bundles, one bundle crisscross, you know, it's like the other, but only two in a place. But a shock of grain, they then have all six, about six bundles in the shock. And that's shocked up and they'll stand up on the field, you know, stand up in the air and that lets it dry.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: One man does that job, goes around shocking?

segments.speaker: Ima Hodge Platz
segments.words: Well, they have different shockers, you know, usually yes, it's only one. But then he's not following that binder, maybe. It's already been bound, you see, and he's gone on. The one that rode the binder, he's gone on to another piece of ground or something, maybe to cut more.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: How long does the grain stand there and dry in the shocks?

segments.speaker: Ima Hodge Platz
segments.words: Well, they just, it all depends on if it's as soon as it's drying up or they like to, as soon as it's cured, they like to thrash it, you know. And that all depends on how quick you can get a thrasher. You see the machine, the thrashing machine is all of its own. And these bundles are made with the binder.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: So it could stand there for a week or more?

segments.speaker: Ima Hodge Platz
segments.words: Oh, it stands over that because it's got to be seasoned. If it's too wet, you see, and then you stack all those wells together, but then you have to mold. And it all depends on the condition of the weather and things. That makes a difference. Sometimes it rains on those buns when they're in the shock and they have to turn those. And that's the job for the farmers I have to do. If it's a lot of rain, why? So that it won't spoil the grain. See, if they were left, why they'd start to grow and sprout.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Is it hard to shock? Is there any trick to piling your bundle so they stand against each other?

segments.speaker: Ima Hodge Platz
segments.words: Yes, I guess there is. I never did shock. But they always put two together, I know, to start the shock. And then they'll stack around those two. And I think the condition the grain is in depends on how many they put in the shock. You see, it'll dry quicker if you don't have too many. And it depends on the weather that comes. And a lot of times if it rains, why? They've got to take and turn those bundles if it rains a whole lot. As soon as they get dry enough in order for it not to sprout.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Well, the thrashing crew that you work with, that didn't include the binder then.

segments.speaker: Ima Hodge Platz
segments.words: No, it didn't include it. After it was in the shock, that didn't include the...

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: So then your harvest crew came along, right?

segments.speaker: Ima Hodge Platz
segments.words: Well, that's when the thrasher come. It was separate ... What cuts the grain, you know, that's all together separate.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: And what did the thrashing crew do then? How did that work?

segments.speaker: Ima Hodge Platz
segments.words: Well, that's the one that takes care of it after it's cut and dried, getting the condition to be thrashed. So you can't just cut it and thrash it right away. It's got season-like.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Well, when your crew started in, when the harvest crew then started with that, how did they go about picking up the shocks?

segments.speaker: Ima Hodge Platz
segments.words: Well, the shocks were already up. They stand up, those bundles do. And you just put your fork in them and put them where you want them. They'd have to haul them to the machine. The bundle haulers have to pick up those shocks and load it on this wagon that they haul it to the machine in. And they have to drive it to where the thrashing machine's set. They just put it in a spot, you know, and they don't move it around and without, they won't have to move to a different field or something. It's interesting to see what they have to do. They don't know what they have to do to get it. That's all a lot of people don't know what it means to harvest. They don't know. They think it's just done right now. Well, it's not. It's a long time. You wait a long time for those crops. So, in the fall or sometimes in the spring and then you don't, after it's cut even, you've got to wait until it's matured. If you just scratch it as soon as it's cut, your grain would be damp and it might spoil on you. So, it's not just a lot of people don't know what it means.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: You say when the pitching of the bundles is not easy, it takes a good knack?

segments.speaker: Ima Hodge Platz
segments.words: Well, it's a knack, yes. It's the size of the bundle is that you've got to pick up off of the ground there and load it up on a bundle wagon. Just pitch it over there. All you have to do is get it in the bed, in the bundle wagon, the bed of the bundle wagon. And that's what the driver that has the team does is to place that bundle after the pitcher pitches it up on the wagon, you see. After you pitch it up, you're done with it. There's another fellow that drives the team to move it, he's the one then that has to place it around on his header bed or on the bed that they hauled in.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Some guys could pitch bundles better than other guys could?

segments.speaker: Ima Hodge Platz
segments.words: Oh, yes. Goodness sakes, yes. Some of them are just easy as could be for them. And others, there's an art in it. And then the fellow drives the team while he'll place it around in the bed where he wants it. See, the bundle, the bed is, well, you've seen the bed. Well, the pitcher just pitches it in there and the one that's in there driving the team, he's the one that places the bundles around on his load. But some fellows have the nicest looking even loads when they come in with their bundles all even, you know. And others, they just throwed there.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: They just what?

segments.speaker: Ima Hodge Platz
segments.words: Just throwed on them. Didn't care, you know, or didn't know or what, I don't know. But some of the loads that when they were loaded on nice, the bundles, they looked nice. And then sitting up there driving, sitting up there driving the horses, looked good to see it. But then when they're just haphazard way of loading, it's shown, told them if they didn't know anything about or didn't care. And that was up to the man that ran the bundle wagon, how the load looked. Well, the one that pitched, it was the one that loaded the bundles after they were pitched onto the wagon, you see. There's a way to place those around in there and you can get more. There's an art in it. A lot of them don't know what it means to, oh, well, it's just like sewing sacks or anything. There's an art in it. You can tell when the bins that come into the machine, the cookhouse wasn't generally very far from the machine. And you can tell anybody that never loaded the bundles onto the wagon because their bundles were even and nice outside. There wasn't one sticking here and another one little, and one way over here. You could tell one that was used to doing that. There's an art in it.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Well, what happened then when they brought it into the machine and how did they get it off the wagon?

segments.speaker: Ima Hodge Platz
segments.words: Well, they had to pitch it off, the fellas that hauled it into the machine while they pitched it over in the feeder on the separator, you see. And they'd generally be, and sometimes a man feeds that. Did you ever see a man feed one? Well, it's an art. The feeder, they pitched those bundles off the wagon on the little table, the side of the machine, you know, up high. And the feeder, why he... Each arm would just go in like that, excuse me, you know. And that pulled it, he pulled his bundle on this side and pulled the bundle over here. And that feeds it into the separator.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What did he use to feed it with? He used it to pitch forward?

segments.speaker: Ima Hodge Platz
segments.words: His hands.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: His hands?

segments.speaker: Ima Hodge Platz
segments.words: He just pulled it into that feeder, you see. It was just a hole in the top of the separator and all this work in here underneath was what took the grain, took the kernels from the straw. They'd just take a hold of the grain, they'd pitch it, usually one from each side, they'd gently... And then the feeder, why he was working his arms just like that, just pulling it in.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did he cut the string around the bundle?

segments.speaker: Ima Hodge Platz
segments.words: No, the bundle, no, you didn't have to cut it. The machine takes that off.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: So he just pushed the whole bundle in?

segments.speaker: Ima Hodge Platz
segments.words: Well, no, he didn't, if it's too big, he didn't, because it plugged up the machine, you see. It could only take so much as... It just made a revolution, you know, and just... They just feed it like that. So he'd push it from... Off of this little table, what they would unload it on with the table there, you know, and that bundle would lay there until that was pushed off that table down here in the machine. And they'd just go like that with their arms.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: From side to side of the table?

segments.speaker: Ima Hodge Platz
segments.words: No, just... Just like this was the hole. And all the machinery part was down in here. And your table was here at the side, your arms just like... Just like this, and then it doesn't push it in there, and push it in here. And there's an art in feeding those things, too.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What's the art in that? How fast you feed it?

segments.speaker: Ima Hodge Platz
segments.words: Yes, how fast and what... Sure. They don't need to think it's no art and nothing one of those separator things. A lot of people don't know. They don't think it means anything, but it does. Now, you can see, their arms are going like this. They'd take a bundle from one side and put it in here, and then they'd take the other bundle, but they didn't put it all in there. They'd wait, you see. See, they just...

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: They'd wait till there was room in the separator to take?

segments.speaker: Ima Hodge Platz
segments.words: Well, yes. But they didn't wait long. It just... About the time they'd get this one off, why they'd bring this one off, see, and just kept their arms going like this.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did they have to work real fast, those men?

segments.speaker: Ima Hodge Platz
segments.words: Oh, no. Just steady. You do that all day long, but you get used to it. It's... And then down here, away, you see out of the rolls of grain, there'd be sack sores down the way, so in the separator. And they'd hang the sacks, it's a place to hang sacks. And then they'd have a jig. That jig's down that grain after it gets in the sack so much why they started jigging it, you know, bouncing it up and down so as to give it all the space there is in there that the grain can get into.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: So there's one man that does that… he's the jigger?

segments.speaker: Ima Hodge Platz
segments.words: Well, yeah, there's one that jigs and then the sack sewer, you see, he's there with his needle.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did you ever see a sack?

segments.speaker: Ima Hodge Platz
segments.words: Well, they're interesting. They're about as long and they're a little crooked.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: The needles are? About as long as your finger?

segments.speaker: Ima Hodge Platz
segments.words: A little longer than your second finger. Well, about like that. And there's a hole in the end of them and they're curved.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Curved on the end?

segments.speaker: Ima Hodge Platz
segments.words: Yeah, well, they're just kind of like that. And the needle and the sack sewer, you just poke that in the jiggy sack. They have usually a jigger on the sacks so as I fill up all the space, you know, won't be a lot of... those sacks cost money too. And this fella that jigs it and just jig it down. And then they'll set it out for the sack sewer to sew, you know.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: How many stitches? Did he put a lot of stitches in the top?

segments.speaker: Ima Hodge Platz
segments.words: Oh, well, it's about that far apart.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Every inch or two?

segments.speaker: Ima Hodge Platz
segments.words: Well, not like that. I wouldn't say just how many but went across the top of the sack, you see. And if you had a good sack sewer, you had something. Some of them, they could just poke that on the needle in just like that. Pull it up.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Could they keep up with the sacks coming out? Could they keep up with the grain?

segments.speaker: Ima Hodge Platz
segments.words: Well, there was usually two on the side. Usually two sewers on the side. See, one of them was a saw in his sack while the other one was there a filling of sack, hanging up a sack, you see. And one man can't sew it and hang it on too. But it's interesting to see how they manage it. The sack sewer...

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Was the sack sewer usually a man?

segments.speaker: Ima Hodge Platz
segments.words: Oh, yes. Well, he was a man or else old enough to handle the sack. He'd have to carry it after it was filled. As a rule. That he'd sew that. The jigger, you see, jigs it down, the grain. So he'd be tightening your sack. And that saves a lot of sacks, you see, if you jig it down. And it needs a good sack sewer. It makes good money.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Sacks sewer was a good-paying job?

segments.speaker: Ima Hodge Platz
segments.words: It was good. A lot of them know they'd sew, but they'd sew too far apart. But the needle in too far apart, and then when it was raised up, I sometimes leak out at the holes in the top. We had a good sack sewer who made good money. It was... Well then, how did the sack...

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: The sacks get piled after that?

segments.speaker: Ima Hodge Platz
segments.words: Well, the men didn't have to carry them away. You see, they'd get them sewed, but they'd carry them to the sack pile. They'd pile them up close. Well, not too close. I suppose they'd estimate about how the grain would go. And they'd carry them... The first ones they carry out, you have to carry farther. And they'd pile them up, build them up. It's not so far to carry them. But then you've got to lift them up a little higher, you see. Get them up on the pile.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: One of those sacks would be pretty heavy?

segments.speaker: Ima Hodge Platz
segments.words: Oh, yeah, it's a rule. They'd weigh over two. Well, some of them would weigh 175 pounds. Yeah, they were heavy. They earned their money. But it's really an art to see them so you wouldn't... You'd just take those little needles and just... You'd think they'd run it in their hand. It's an art.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: You'd think they'd run it in their hand?

segments.speaker: Ima Hodge Platz
segments.words: I'd say you'd think they would. No, they don't run it in their hand. No. But there's an art in sewing. And a good sack sawed. And Jen, who got good wages.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What about the other men who were on the crew? There was a separator tender, was there?

segments.speaker: Ima Hodge Platz
segments.words: Yes, separator tender and then tender.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What did those men do?

segments.speaker: Ima Hodge Platz
segments.words: Oh, well, they just tended to the separator. You know, they were really, too. But then if anything went wrong, they got to watch because sometimes the things that kind of plug up, you know, they don't get the feeders. The feed the grain into the machine. You see the picture, the bundle hauler. They have those shelves up here. I call it a shelf, but it's part of the separator. And they throw it. It's just for the bundle to light to from the bundle wagon. And they just go like that all the time, you know. They load a wagon on each side of the separator, see. These two are working there all the same time. And they just pitch. And on this side would come the bundle. And over here, you know, that's the way the feeder had it.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: But then the separator tender, he'd look after if something went wrong?

segments.speaker: Ima Hodge Platz
segments.words: Oh, yes, if anything went wrong. It's just like that. Your feet, they were just working their arms like that. With the bundle of grain underneath each arm, see. And you're just poking it in this feeder here.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: The engineer, what did he do? What was his job?

segments.speaker: Ima Hodge Platz
segments.words: Well, his job was take care of the engineer. And they had their jobs. But, and you never know, something can go wrong or something. You pretty soon maybe everything going along and it all, and it all depends on what went into the feeder spot. You know, sometimes it'd be something maybe in the grain, in the shock of grain or bundle of grain. It'd be something, you know, that the feeder wouldn't take. And you had to watch. Anything you'd hear grinding noise for, they was a horn. They had, a lot of times, it would break to some of the cylinders, I suppose, or something.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What did they do? They shut the machine down?

segments.speaker: Ima Hodge Platz
segments.words: Oh, yes. They'd shut it down as quick as possible when they'd hear the noise, you know, when something wasn't right. But they hollered loud enough that you'd know. It's really interesting to see them.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did you ever see fires in the field when you were working there?

segments.speaker: Ima Hodge Platz
segments.words: No, I never did, but then they had fires, but we never did. They're not that I ever saw. This girl and I went seven years for one man and harvested seven different harvests.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What was his name again?

segments.speaker: Ima Hodge Platz
segments.words: Ed Parker.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: And this was near Viola?

segments.speaker: Ima Hodge Platz
segments.words: Yes. Maybe you know Jimmy Parker. He lives in Palouse. I don't think, I don't believe I do. I went to school with him. But Ed was his brother, but he was an older person. But it's really interesting. You just wonder how they ever get it to go and how they could ever figure it out, I don't know.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Figured out how to do all that?

segments.speaker: Ima Hodge Platz
segments.words: So everything just came in, you know, those feeders. The men that fed, there was just like a table up here and they was cheering between. And there was a bunch of horse that would unload their bundle off of their wagon onto this table. And that was one on each side, you see. And the feeder just going like that all the time.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: I want to ask you again about the cooking that you had to do there in the cook house and how that worked. You said there were only two of you that did all that cooking?

segments.speaker: Ima Hodge Platz
segments.words: Yes, there was only two of us that did all the cooking.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: And when did you start in the morning?

segments.speaker: Ima Hodge Platz
segments.words: Two thirty. Got up at two thirty. We had breakfast at four o 'clock.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What did it take for you to get the breakfast ready from when you got up? What did you have to do to get it on the table?

segments.speaker: Ima Hodge Platz
segments.words: Well, we had to cook it. Cook potatoes and make biscuits and make gravy. Fried beef, a pan of beef steak. When we didn't have bacon, we used to have beef steak.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: And you and she divided it up and each of you took about half the work, is that how it worked?

segments.speaker: Ima Hodge Platz
segments.words: Well, I made the bread and she took care of the meat. Each one we had her own job. She took care of the meat and the rest of it by whoever needed to do what they had done. We went seven years together, seven harvests. And we were hired from the time we were pulled in one year to the next. For the next. We had the job already. To the next.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Now what was the trouble when you say the wagon, they'd move the wagon from place to place? The cook house?

segments.speaker: Ima Hodge Platz
segments.words: Well, they'd move the cook house to different fields, you know. They'd thrash for different people. The grain. Wherever the grain was, the cook house was there too. And they'd move the cook house. And there you had to pack your stuff in the cook house. Maybe you'd be well, I'd bake bread on the road different times. Maybe just get it in the oven, a little while before and you'd think it'd never be fit to eat. You'd wonder. But they'd generally eat you.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What would you have to do while they were moving it?

segments.speaker: Ima Hodge Platz
segments.words: Well, we'd stay in the cook house and ride. Maybe pee a sponge or something.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: And hold the bread in the oven, you say?

segments.speaker: Ima Hodge Platz
segments.words: Yeah, we'd stand and hold the oven door shut over a round because if we didn't, the door would come down and the bread would slide out.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: And you didn't wind up getting sick to your stomach by the time that moved it?

segments.speaker: Ima Hodge Platz
segments.words: No, we didn't wind up no better. We couldn't do anything good to get sick. That'd be worse. Hammer all that beef steak for them to have for breakfast.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did you decide what the menu was going to be yourselves?

segments.speaker: Ima Hodge Platz
segments.words: Oh, yeah.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: You ordered the food you wanted?

segments.speaker: Ima Hodge Platz
segments.words: Yes, we did have one or more. Yeah, we decided on that.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did you think that the food was real good on those crews? I mean, did the men eat real well?

segments.speaker: Ima Hodge Platz
segments.words: Well, I thought I'd ... Yeah, I think it was. It's good as we could fix it anyway. We seemed to be satisfied that the boss must have been satisfied. We went seven years for him. It's a session each harvest.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What did you think the work, what was the working, what was the conditions like for you to work under? I mean, were they real hard on a person to, was it hard, tough for a person to cook in that kind of a setting where you didn't have much but a little?

segments.speaker: Ima Hodge Platz
segments.words: Well, it wasn't like it was where you had a home or something, but then we had plenty to cook with and plenty to eat it. So I guess they liked it.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: It was very hot?

segments.speaker: Ima Hodge Platz
segments.words: Not too bad, because we could raise the sides of the cookhouse, the curtain on the side we could raise and make a draft through. And there was a door in each end, so it wasn't too bad. Sometimes it's kind of hot, but it wasn't too bad. After you got used to it.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What was the big meal of the day?

segments.speaker: Ima Hodge Platz
segments.words: All of them… don't make this much difference. We usually had pie for dinner. Sometimes we'd just get bread nailing or cake or something and they'd come over the hill with the team. Had to move. Not for something. It's wonder they'd eat the food at the door.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What about the dust? Was the dust bad while they were working in the field?

segments.speaker: Ima Hodge Platz
segments.words: Oh, not too bad, no. It wasn't. She was in stubble mostly, so that'd make a difference. Well, there'd be some. It wasn't like they could expect it. They just swelled.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: And about what time would you think you got to bed at night? Got to go to sleep. When would you be finished with all this work?

segments.speaker: Ima Hodge Platz
segments.words: Oh, well, we'd have breakfast. We had to prepare for breakfast the night before, you know. So we wouldn't have as much to do next morning. I don't know. We'd get to bed about after 10 or something like that.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: So you only got about four hours' sleep?

segments.speaker: Ima Hodge Platz
segments.words:
Not very long. You get used to it. 
Sam Schrager,00:34:59,Sounds like when you went to sleep you met yourself getting up the next morning. We did. We had plenty to cook and everything.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Would you say that it was hard work for the men in the field? That it was hard working at the harvest?

segments.speaker: Ima Hodge Platz
segments.words: Well, it's just it's your pitching. A lot of the men that handle the ...wagons, why, it's just like you're pitching on them. When they come, why, you'd have to load up the drivers. It's, you know, you've been working. But a lot of times some can do it easier than others. Well, they don't want to go out in the harvest field and think that they won't have to work.

segments.speaker: Unknown Speaker
segments.words: NURSE!

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Would you like me to get her?

segments.speaker: Ima Hodge Platz
segments.words: I've got to help. This moment. ... Two and a half. Two and a half.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: It's not bad wages, was it?

segments.speaker: Ima Hodge Platz
segments.words: Well, no. Because he paid us more than some of the others were getting. No. We worked seven years for that one man.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Was that about what the men were getting in the fields? A day?

segments.speaker: Ima Hodge Platz
segments.words: Something like that.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Two and a half?

segments.speaker: Ima Hodge Platz
segments.words: Yeah… that wasn't the way, like the wages are now. But that was higher than most others got. We worked seven years for him. It was hard for ... to pull in the fall for the next year. So he must have been satisfied.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: You mean, he hired you as soon as you got there for the year that was going to be the next one?

segments.speaker: Ima Hodge Platz
segments.words: Well, when he pulled in that year, why he spoke hard for the next year.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: The following brief section is Alvin Olson of Deary, Iowa. Remembering old Joe Wells.

segments.speaker: Alvin Olson
segments.words: He used to say, I'm the only white man here that rests were Swedes! Yeah, he was a good fellow. My dad, we used to go and disturb George, all of your wells there. And when we'd come by, he'd say, there wasn't just some crepes and wood where to go by. Joe Wells was placed where he went for Troy. When he sees us coming, he'd come up, have us to come in, and have us to come in and give us a feed. Joe Wells, he was the best fellow around here. He was, that's what everybody said. He was real good. And he had two boys, Chuck and Roy, and a daughter, Mary. But they're all gone now, you know. When he sees who lives on that place, no, I don't know.
